candidate_relations.reason: The mild thrombocytopenia predates olaparib and is a laboratory finding rather than the fingertip purpuric drug eruption.
The record supports a localized olaparib-induced cutaneous eruption, not a primary bleeding disorder.
Chronic mild thrombocytopenia without an immune workup does not establish immune thrombocytopenic purpura.
Olaparib is implicated, but the documented adverse event is a purpuric drug eruption rather than new drug-induced thrombocytopenia.
There is no heparin exposure or acute platelet fall to support heparin-induced thrombocytopenia.
BRCA1-related prostate cancer explains olaparib use but is not the diagnosed skin eruption.
Localized painless purpura without systemic illness or coagulation findings does not indicate disseminated intravascular coagulation.
The record provides no basis for attributing the longstanding mild thrombocytopenia to BRCA1.
The stable historical thrombocytopenia and localized eruption do not establish immune thrombocytopenia.
Nonpalpable fingertip purpura without systemic features is not Henoch-Schönlein purpura.
No immune-mediated platelet destruction is documented, and the target diagnosis is a drug eruption.
The record has no monoclonal gammopathy or other evidence of Waldenström macroglobulinemia.
There is no hemolysis, severe thrombocytopenia, renal-neurologic syndrome, or fever pattern supporting TTP.
The faint nonpalpable lesions and drug timing support a purpuric drug eruption rather than vasculitis.
Drug toxicity is compatible with olaparib causation but omits the purpuric cutaneous phenotype.
Metastatic prostate cancer is the treatment context and not the fingertip eruption.
The platelet count was similarly low years earlier and does not define the olaparib-induced eruption.
Purpura names the manifestation but omits olaparib causation and the drug-eruption diagnosis.
The close temporal relationship to olaparib supports a drug eruption rather than a paraneoplastic syndrome.
Mild stable cytopenias without marrow evidence do not establish bone marrow failure.
